etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French contester, from Old French, from Latin contestor (“to call to witness”).

quote.citation: 1725, Homer, “Book IV”, in [Elijah Fenton], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], volume I, London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC:
quote.text: Of man, who dares in pomp with Jove contest?

quote.citation: 1684-1690, Thomas Burnet, Sacred Theory of the Earth
quote.text: As for the difficulty or obscurity of an argument, that does but add to the pleasure.of contesting with it when there are hopes of victory

definitions.definition: (transitive) To call into question; to oppose.

quote.citation: 1848, John Daniel Morell, Historical and Critical View of the Speculative Philosophy of Europe in the Nineteenth Century:
quote.text: Few philosophical aphorisms have been more frequently repeated, few more contested than this.

quote.citation: 1981, Anouar Abdel-Malek, Social Dialectics: Nation and Revolution, page 13:
quote.text: On the other hand, the nationalitarian phenomenon is one in which the struggle against the imperialist powers of occupation has as its object, beyond the clearing of the national territory, the independence and sovereignty of the national State, uprooting in depth the positions of the ex-colonial power— the reconquest of the power of decision in all domains of national life, the prelude to that reconquest of identity  which is at the heart of the renaissance undertaken on the basis of fundamental national demands, and ceaselessly contested, by every means available, on every level, and notably on the internal level'.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To strive earnestly to hold or maintain; to struggle to defend.
(law) To make a subject of litigation; to defend, as a suit; to dispute or resist, as a claim, by course of law.
